newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar sinks below 111 yen in Tokyo on trade fears.
newsitem.headline: Dollar sinks below 111 yen in Tokyo on trade fears.

text.p: The dollar sank briefly below 111 yen in Tokyo on Wednesday, its lowest level in nearly seven months, after comments by a senior U.S. official and a big jump in Japan's external surplus fanned trade friction fears.
Waves of selling pushed the U.S. currency to 110.97 yen before it recovered to about 111.45 yen just after midday.
Dealers said the greenback, which closed in New York around 112.20 on Tuesday, remained vulnerable and could fall sharply if and when it slid below the key 110 level.
Remarks by U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers, close on the heels of news Japan's current account surplus nearly doubled in April, triggered the sharp dollar drop.

In a prepared speech for delivery to a trade group in Denver, Colorado, Summers urged Japan to foster a domestic demand-led economic recovery at home, to avoid running up external surpluses that would hurt global growth, and to keep up efforts to deregulate and open its markets to foreign goods.

Fears Japan's resurgent surplus will grab attention when leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrial nations meet in Denver later this month are making currency market players jittery, although some U.S. officials have said the summit was not likely to dwell on the topic at length.

Japan's Finance Ministry said on Wednesday that the surplus in its current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose 92.7 percent to 1.09 trillion yen ($9.7 billion) in April from a year earlier, while the surplus in merchandise trade alone rose 90.9 percent to 1.02 trillion yen ($9.1 billion),

Economists attributed the rise to an April 1 increase in Japan's national sales tax, which dampened consumption of all goods, including imports, while a strong U.S. economy sucked in Japanese exports.
The greenback first rose after the current account and trade figures proved in line with most private forecasts, but resumed its downward march after Summers' comments.
Japan's "Mr Yen," influential Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara, greeted the yen's latest rise by reiterating Tokyo's dislike of sharp currency swings.
"Both an excessively weak yen and an excessively strong yen are undesirable," Jiji news agency quoted Sakakibara as saying.

Some experts believe Tokyo is less concerned about the yen's level against the dollar than the pace of its gains, and traders are speculating that it will let the yen rise to around 110 to the dollar ahead of the G7 summit in a show of good faith that it does not want its surplus to surge.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on Tuesday expressed concern about what she called "disturbing" trends in Japan's trade balance and repeated that Washington did not want a big rise in Japan's surplus.
"We have communicated to Japan we do not expect to see any significant increase in the current account surplus as Japan begins to deregulate its economy," she told a House panel.
White House economist Janet Yellen, however, told reporters the same day that Tokyo did not appear to be relying on foreign sales as a source of growth.

Japanese government bond futures contracts rose after the yen's surge, while Tokyo share prices eased somewhat on concern about damage to exporters' profits. A strong yen makes Japanese products less price-competitive abroad.
The 225-share Nikkei average finished the morning session down 99.01 points, or 0.48 percent, at 20,433.54.
